This verse, spoken by the jinn, reports that men among the humans used to seek refuge with lords of the jinn when they camped in a desolate valley in pre-Islamic times, saying: I seek refuge with the chief of this valley from the foolish ones of his people, and they would spend the night under its protection. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that this custom was well known among the Arabs. The meaning of the last phrase is debated. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand it as an increase in sin, since the humans strengthened the jinn in their beliefs. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari take it to mean that the jinn increased the humans in fear or boldness towards them. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Abu al-Aliya and others hold that the humans increased the jinn in pride, as they said: we rule over humans and jinn. Al-Tabari notes that rahaq in Arabic means sin and the violation of what is forbidden. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy, note that the pronoun may refer to either group. Ibn Kathir mentions a report in which the wolf that carried off a lamb may have been a jinn, without deciding the question. Many commentators see in the verse a condemnation of seeking protection from other than God.

This verse reports the words of the jinn after they heard the Quran: the disbelievers among humans had the same assumption as they did, namely that God would send no one to be raised up. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as referring to the human unbelievers who denied that God would send a messenger, and they link this denial to rejecting the resurrection. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take the pronoun as referring to the human disbelievers, while the address in 'you assumed' is the jinn speaking among themselves. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Shawkani instead consider the verse part of God's own speech addressed to the Quraysh, with 'you' meaning them. Al-Razi inclines to treat it as the jinn's own words, since that fits the surrounding discourse. Scholars also differ on the meaning of 'raising up': al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi allow either the sending of a prophet or the resurrection of the dead for judgment, while Ibn Ashur finds the sending of messengers the better fit for the context. Ibn Sa'di notes that this denial led people to polytheism and transgression. Al-Jaza'iri observes that the jinn believed in the Quran after hearing only a little of it, whereas the human disbelievers rejected it.

In this verse the jinn describe what they found when they tried to reach the sky to eavesdrop: it was filled with strong guards and with burning meteors. The commentators agree that the word 'touch' here means seeking or attempting to reach, that 'haras' is a collective noun in the singular, and that the 'shuhub' are bright stars hurled at anyone who tries to overhear. They also agree that the jinn once sat in certain places of the sky to listen, then passed what they heard to soothsayers who added falsehoods. The disagreement concerns when these projectiles began. Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Qutayba, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir hold that the hurling increased and the guard was tightened at the time of the Prophet's mission, relying on the report in which the Prophet asks his companions what they used to say when a star fell in the Jahiliyya. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Ashur hold instead that the phenomenon was known before the mission and only grew stronger afterwards, citing pre-Islamic verses. Al-Jahiz denies that any hurling took place before the mission, but al-Razi and al-Qurtubi reply to him with the same evidence. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari stress that the verse speaks of filling and increase rather than of the origin of the hurling. Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn and al-Shawkani see the guard as a protection of the Quran against distortion. All agree that the jinn understood that a great event had occurred on earth.

This verse reports what the jinn said after hearing the Qur'an: before, they used to sit in places in the heavens to listen in, but now anyone who tries to listen finds a watching meteor waiting for him. The commentators agree that the guards (haras) are angels and the shuhub are burning stars that drive away the devils, and that the watch over the heavens became much stricter with the Prophet's mission, to the point of cutting off eavesdropping entirely. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir report that such stars were already thrown before prophethood, but that the practice intensified afterwards. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi also hold this earlier existence and cite verses of pre-Islamic poets such as Aws ibn Hajar and Bishr ibn Abi Khazim. Al-Jahiz, by contrast, considers these verses fabricated and holds that stoning did not occur before prophethood, a view Ibn al-Jawzi adopts. Al-Razi explains that the word lamasa means seeking, a common metaphor, while most read rasadan as an adjective for the meteor meaning lying in wait, or as a collective noun for the angels who hurl them, and Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as a verbal noun. Modern commentators see in the passage a refutation of the claim by soothsayers to know the unseen.

In this verse the jinn describe their bewilderment after they were prevented from eavesdropping on the heavens. They say they do not know whether God intends evil for the people of the earth, meaning punishment or abandonment, or whether He intends for them right guidance, meaning good and direction. The commentators note a fine courtesy in the wording: evil is expressed in the passive with no stated agent, while good is attributed directly to God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the jinn, seeing the sky guarded by sentinels and shooting stars, thought this presaged either a sudden punishment for mankind or the sending of a guiding prophet. Al-Tabari considers the verse part of the account of eavesdropping that precedes it. Al-Kalbi explains the meaning as that people will either obey this messenger and be guided, or disobey him and be destroyed. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the question as concerning how people will respond to this prophet: whether they will believe and be guided, or deny him and suffer harm. Ibn Zayd identifies the evil as the pelting with shooting stars itself. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the jinn may have spoken these words before hearing the Qur'an, or afterwards, when they returned to their people as warners. The commentaries agree on the jinn's perplexity at the changed state of the sky and on the courtesy of the phrasing, which Ibn Sa'di and Abu al-Su'ud link to reverence toward God.

In this verse the jinn describe their condition before they heard the Qur'an. They say that some of them are righteous and others are below that level, and that they were divided into many paths and sects. Commentators agree that the righteous are those upright in faith and conduct, and that those below them have not reached full righteousness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the paths are doctrines or inclinations and the qidad are scattered groups. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrimah and Qatadah take them to be divergent desires, while Mujahid says the jinn were Muslims and disbelievers. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi list sects such as Qadariyya, Murji'a, Rafida and Khawarij. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi discuss the grammar, especially the omitted noun and the meaning of dun, which some read as meaning other than. Al-Qurtubi argues that the jinn were not all unbelievers, since some believed in Musa and Isa, and he holds this reading to be the most sound. All agree that these words are the jinn's own speech, describing their state before faith, and that the verse prepares the report of their belief in the Qur'an and their pursuit of right guidance.

In this verse the jinn state their conviction, after hearing the Qur'an, that they could neither escape God on earth nor overcome Him by fleeing: He is able to reach them wherever they are if He wills them harm. Most commentators take the verb "zanna" here in the sense of certain knowledge. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that they cannot outrun God, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi treat "on earth" and "fleeing" as circumstantial phrases, meaning that they cannot escape Him whether they remain on earth or flee upward to the heavens. Al-Razi notes that the words may mean that flight would be useless, while Ibn 'Ashur stresses the sense of a heavenly punishment that cannot be evaded. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi also note that the jinn's certainty may be described either before or after their conversion, depending on the reading. The commentators agree on God's greatness and power and on the impossibility of escaping Him for any human or jinn. They differ on the grammatical construction of the sentence and on the precise meaning of the flight mentioned. None of them decides between these readings, all of which remain accepted.

In this verse the jinn describe how, after hearing the Guidance, which is the Qur'an that leads to the straight path, they believed in it and affirmed that it comes from God. Whoever believes in his Lord, they say, fears neither a reduction of his good deeds nor the burden of a sin that is not his. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain bakhs as the loss of good deeds and rahaq as an increase in bad deeds, while Ibn Zayd and al-Nasafi understand rahaq as injustice or humiliation. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the believer suffers neither a loss of reward nor injustice, since he has wronged no one. On the rest of the passage, the commentators agree that the jinn are divided into different groups: Mujahid distinguishes Muslims from disbelievers, while al-Hasan and al-Suddi mention sects such as the Qadariyya, the Murji'a and the Rafida. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba read the tara'iq as divergent opinions and creeds. Regarding the reading of the hamza in inna, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur observe that it may follow the verb of speech or the phrase fa-amanna bihi, which slightly changes the grammar. Ibn al-Qayyim takes from this verse that believing jinn enter Paradise and disbelievers enter Hell, an argument also cited by al-Bukhari, and no other commentator disputes it. The overall meaning is an encouragement to faith and uprightness.

In this verse the jinn report what they said to their people after hearing the Qur'an: among them are Muslims who submit to God in obedience, and among them are the qasitun, those who are unjust and turn away from the truth. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain that the qasitun are disbelievers or those who deviate from the right path, while Ibn 'Abbas describes them as those who set up equals to God. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain the root meaning: qasata means to act unjustly, and aqsata to act justly. Al-Razi relates the story of Sa'id ibn Jubayr before al-Hajjaj, who was called a qasit and took it as praise, though the word means unjust. The commentators agree that whoever submits has sought the right path, and that the unjust will be fuel for Hell. Ibn 'Atiyya suggests that the sentence may be God's own words rather than the jinn's, and al-Zamakhshari argues from it that God is too just to punish the unjust without rewarding the one who follows the right path, an argument others reject by denying the jinn any reward. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that the verses that follow are not the jinn's speech. Ibn al-Qayyim divides the jinn into righteous, those below them, and disbelievers. The word tahharaw, meaning to seek with care and aim at what is right, is agreed upon by the commentators.

This passage from Surah al-Jinn gives the words of the jinn after they heard the Quran. Among them are Muslims who submit to God in obedience, and qasitun, those who depart unjustly from the truth and from the path of Islam. Most commentators understand the qasitun as the disbelievers. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain the word as meaning those who deviate from the truth or are wrongdoers, and al-Tabari, followed by al-Farra', notes that the qasit is the one who acts unjustly while the muqsit is the just one. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir state that those who submitted to Islam have sought the right direction, whereas the qasitun will be fuel for Hell, which is kindled by them just as it is by disbelieving humans. The scholars differ on who is speaking in the phrase about whoever submits and seeks guidance: Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as God addressing His Prophet, while others take it as the jinns' own speech. Al-Zamakhshari also reports that some who denied the jinns any reward relied on this verse, but he replies that God is too just to punish the qasit without rewarding the one who is rightly guided. Ibn al-Qayyim links this three-part division to the division of humankind into the righteous, the middling and the disbelievers.

This verse from Surat al-Jinn, as the commentators explain it, means that if those who had deviated from the truth had kept to the straight path, God would have given them abundant water, meaning abundant provision, since water is the root of livelihood. He would test them with this blessing to see whether they would give thanks or disbelieve. He then warns that whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, meaning the Qur'an and worship, will be made to undergo a harsh punishment with no respite. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, understand the path to be Islam, guidance and obedience, so that uprightness brings good and blessing in this world. Others, such as Abu Mijlaz, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Kalbi, take the path to be the way of disbelief, in which case the widening of provision is a respite that leads them into trial before punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi favour the first reading, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers the second less consistent with the word for uprightness. On the meaning of trial, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir explain it as a test, while others take it as a temptation by wealth, citing 'Umar's saying that wherever there is water there is wealth, and wherever there is wealth there is trial. The word sa'ad has been explained by Ibn 'Abbas as a mountain in hell and by others as a painful hardship, the sense the lexicographers prefer.

This passage from Surah al-Jinn explains that, according to what was revealed to the Prophet, God would have given people abundant water had they remained upright on the path, and that this bounty is a trial to test their gratitude. Whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord will be led into a grievous punishment. The commentators agree on the meaning of ghadaq as abundant water, on sa'ad as a difficult and overwhelming torment, and on fitna as a test. They differ, however, on which uprightness is meant and on what the pronoun refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Tabari understand uprightness as steadfastness in Islam and obedience, so the water stands for abundance of provision, and they cite verses such as the one on people of the towns who believed. Abu Mijlaz, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Kalbi and Ibn Kaysan take uprightness to mean steadfastness in disbelief, so that wealth would be a respite and a snare for the unbelievers, citing the verse about those who forgot what they were reminded of. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya find the first reading clearer, since uprightness is hardly a fitting word for disbelief. A saying attributed to 'Umar is often quoted: wherever there is water there is wealth, and wherever there is wealth there is trial. On the word sa'ad, Ibn 'Abbas took it to be a mountain in hell, while most exegetes read it as a hardship without respite. The readings differ on whether the verb is nuslikuhu or yuslikuhu, which does not change the essential meaning.

The commentators explain that the verse means that mosques, the places built for prayer and the remembrance of God, belong to God alone, so no one should be invoked or worshipped alongside Him there. They differ on what 'mosques' refers to. Most, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, take it as places of worship in general; Qatada adds that Jews and Christians associated others with God in their churches, so Muslims are commanded to be sincere on entering the mosque. Al-Hasan extends it to the whole earth, which became a mosque for this community. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Talq ibn Habib and Ibn 'Ata understand it as the seven limbs used in prostration, which must prostrate only to God. Others, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, mean the Sacred Mosque or Mecca. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi consider the first meaning the most apparent. According to one report, the jinn asked the Prophet how they could attend prayer so far away, and the verse was revealed. The following phrase, 'when the servant of God stood up to call upon Him, they nearly crowded upon him en masse', is read in two main ways. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak say the jinn pressed around to hear the Qur'an; al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd say humans and jinn united against God's light, yet God would give it victory. Al-Tabari prefers the latter reading, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr sees it as the jinn's words to their people. Readings also differ on 'lubadan' and on whether the initial 'anna' is opened or pronounced with a kasra; the majority read it with a fatha.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Prophet ﷺ standing to worship and call upon God, while a crowd pressed around him until they almost piled upon one another like the matted layers of felt. Most identify 'the servant of God' as the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who was praying and reciting the Quran at Batn Nakhla. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take the pronoun in 'kadu' to refer to the jinn, who crowded in eagerness to hear the Quran. Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd understand it as humans and jinn banding together against him to extinguish God's light, but God refused except to make His light prevail; al-Tabari judges this the most sound reading. Another view, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj, holds that the jinn were amazed at the obedience of his companions who bowed and prostrated behind him, and reported this to their people. On the meaning of 'libadan', Ibn 'Abbas says 'helpers', while Mujahid and most commentators say 'massed groups piled one upon another'. The recitations differ over the vowel of the hamza in 'inna' and of the lam, but most note that the meaning changes little. Some point out that the verse exalts the dignity of servanthood to God, since the Prophet is named by that title here.

This verse records the Prophet ﷺ declaring that he worships only his Lord and associates no one with Him. The commentators draw from it that this declaration is neither strange nor deserving of astonishment, nor a reason for the people to unite against him, as az-Zamakhshari, an-Nasafi and Abu as-Su'ud note. All agree that the speaker in the verse is the Prophet, and the two readings, the imperative “qul” (Hamza, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far) and the past “qala” (the majority), are both accepted as valid.

The commentators report the context: according to Muqatil, the Quraysh told him that he had brought a grave matter and that they would protect him if he gave it up; at-Tabari cites a report in which a jinn chief offered to protect him. The Prophet replies that he holds no power to harm or guide them, that no one can shield him from God, and that he will find no refuge apart from Him. On the meaning of “rashad” and “darr”, opinions differ: some take them as benefit and harm, others as error and guidance, others as punishment and bliss, or death and life. For “multahad”, Qatada and as-Suddi understand a refuge or shelter, al-Kalbi a passage into the earth like a burrow, and at-Tabari a helper.

On the exception “except a message from God”, al-Kalbi reads it as an exception to the preceding clause, while Muqatil reads it as a condition: no one will protect him unless he delivers the message. For all of them, the delivery of the message is what the Prophet can accomplish and what protects him.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to tell the Meccan polytheists that he possesses neither harm nor right guidance for them, since all of that belongs to God alone, and that he is only a servant who cannot do anything of the kind by himself. The commentators agree that the Prophet disclaims any power over harm or rectitude, and that all power belongs to God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that harm and guidance concern both this world and the religion, and Ibn Kathir adds that the Prophet is a human like them, to whom revelation is given, with no share in their guidance or misguidance. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that harm may mean misguidance and rectitude may mean benefit, so the sense is that he can neither harm nor benefit them, a reading supported by Ubayy's recitation ("misguidance and rectitude"). Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list four senses of rectitude: punishment and blessing, death and life, or error and guidance. As for the words "no one can protect me from God," al-Zamakhshari treats them as a parenthetical clause affirming his helplessness, and he explains that the only protection is delivering the message, as al-Hasan and Muqatil say. Most scholars take "refuge" (multahad) to mean a shelter, al-Suddi a hiding place, and al-Kalbi a tunnel in the earth like a burrow. The verse closes with a warning that disobeying God and His messenger leads to Hell, which Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di read as referring to disbelief rather than ordinary sin.

The verse has the Prophet say that no one can shield him from God if he disobeys Him, and that he would find no refuge outside God. The commentators agree on this plain meaning: no protector can save a person from God's punishment, and the Prophet's only duty is to deliver the message. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain it in this general sense, and al-Nasafi links the refusal of protection to disobedience.

The word mulhad is explained in several ways. Qatada, Mujahid and al-Suddi, as reported by al-Tabari and al-Baghawi, take it to mean a shelter or place of refuge, while al-Kalbi describes an opening into the earth like a burrow, a view repeated by al-Razi and al-Qurtubi. Others, including Abu Sa'id and another report from Qatada, take it to mean a protector or ally. Al-Mawardi offers two readings of the first clause: that no one can protect him alongside God's protection, or that no one can protect him from what God has decreed. Al-Zamakhshari treats the sentence as an aside that stresses the Prophet's lack of power.

The exception, "except a message from God," is also read in more than one way. Al-Hasan, cited by al-Baghawi, says the message itself brings security and salvation; Qatada says it is what the Prophet can do with God's help; al-Farra and Ibn Juzayy present it as an exception to the earlier denial of power, with Ibn Juzayy noting the possibility of a separate clause. As for the occasion, al-Sam'ani and al-Qurtubi report that during the night of the Jinn, a Jinn leader named Wirdan offered to push back the crowd around the Prophet. Al-Baghawi and al-Razi report that Quraysh offered him protection if he gave up his call, and the verse answers that offer.

This verse reports that the Prophet ﷺ tells the Meccan polytheists that he possesses for them neither harm nor guidance, and that he holds only the duty to convey God's message and His messages; whoever disobeys God and His Messenger will have the Fire of Hell, remaining in it forever. The commentators differ on the meaning of the exception 'except a conveyance'. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, followed by others, read it as a disconnected exception or as a substitute for 'refuge', meaning that there is no shelter except conveying what he was sent with. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil link it to 'I possess not', so that his only power is to convey. Al-Tabari holds that guidance and misguidance belong to God alone. Al-Farra' also suggested that 'except' means 'if not', so that if he does not convey, he finds no refuge, a reading taken up by Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi. As to disobedience, the majority, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, understand it as disbelief and associating partners with God. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari report that the Mu'tazilites apply it to sinning believers, but this reading is rejected because the context concerns unbelievers. Finally, the commentators connect the following verses to a warning: the disbelievers will see what is promised to them and will know who is weakest in support and smallest in number.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the statement that the Prophet ﷺ has no power to harm or guide his people, and that whoever disobeys God and His Messenger will enter the fire of Hell. The plain meaning is that when they witness what they have been promised, they will then know which side has the weaker helper and the smaller number. They differ on what is promised. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others take it to be the Day of Resurrection, while Qatada and others take it to be punishment in this world. Al-Samani notes that the weakness of helpers and the smallness of numbers will show in the next life, when each person reaches his abode, and he reports an interpretation that God will give the believers wives, children and houris in abundance. Al-Zamakhshari links "until" to the phrase "they will be a massed band against him": they gang up on the Prophet, despise his supporters and count their small number, until they see what they were promised. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan consider that linking it to that phrase is too distant, and prefer to see it as the end point of the judgement of the fire stated earlier. Al-Razi hesitates between the Battle of Badr and the Day of Resurrection. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the disbelievers mocked both promises of victory and threats of punishment, and that the verse shows the failure of their illusions. The commentators agree that the disbelievers will have no helper at that time, that the believers will be supported by God, and that the timing of this promise is part of the unseen that God alone knows.

God tells His Prophet to say to the idolaters that he does not know whether the punishment promised them is near or whether his Lord will set a distant term for it. Knowledge of the timing of the threat belongs to the unseen, which God alone knows: He is the Knower of the unseen and does not reveal it to anyone except a messenger He has chosen, to whom He discloses what He wills. Angels guard him from before and behind, so that devils cannot steal the revelation and pass it to their soothsayers. The commentators differ on who is meant by 'that he may know'. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ma'mar take it to be the Prophet, who learns that earlier messengers delivered their Lord's message and were protected; al-Tabari judges this the most correct view. Mujahid holds it refers to those who denied the messengers, Sa'id ibn Jubayr to Gabriel and his companions, Ibn Qutayba to the jinn, while al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kathir incline to God Himself. On the number of guardians, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Qatada say four angels, while al-Farra' considers that Gabriel is meant. As for the exception, most hold that only messengers receive part of the hidden knowledge. Al-Razi restricts the verse to the Hour alone, while al-Zamakhshari concludes from it that saints' miracles are denied, an objection answered by Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, who distinguish complete knowledge reserved for prophets from partial insights granted to others. The passage ends by affirming that God encompasses and counts all things.

The commentators explain that God alone knows the unseen, and that He does not disclose it to anyone except a messenger He has chosen, to whom He reveals what He wills of it so that this serves as proof of his prophethood. The Prophet ﷺ was told to say to the polytheists that he does not know whether the threatened punishment is near or whether his Lord will set for it a distant term. Most scholars agree that the exception, "except whom He has approved of the messengers," refers to the messengers chosen for prophethood, regarding matters connected with their mission. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the "rasad" as angels who guard the Prophet from the jinn and devils, while Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd describe guards before and behind him; Qatada and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab speak of four angels, whereas al-Farra' takes it to mean Gabriel. On the phrase "so that He may know", opinions differ: al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean that the Prophet should know that earlier messengers had delivered their message; Mujahid takes it to mean that those who denied the messengers should know this; Ibn Jubayr says it means that the Prophet should know Gabriel had conveyed the revelation; and al-Zamakhshari reads it as God's own knowledge. All agree that God encompasses what is with the messengers and has counted everything. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi draw from the verse an argument against the miracles of saints and against soothsaying and astrology, though al-Razi says the verse does not explicitly establish this and that the exception may be read as disjunctive, relating to the Hour of resurrection. He also notes that the verse does not, in his view, exclude every true insight granted to others.

The commentators explain that this verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to the disbelievers that he does not know whether the promised punishment is near or whether his Lord will set a distant term, since knowledge of the unseen belongs to God alone. God does not reveal His unseen to anyone except a messenger He has chosen, and He reveals to him what He wills, which confirms the truth of his mission. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and most exegetes agree that this messenger is guarded by angels placed before and behind him, so that devils cannot steal the revelation, mix falsehood into it, or pass it on to soothsayers. As for the phrase "so that He may know", most, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, take it to refer to the Prophet, who would know that earlier messengers had delivered their Lord's message; Mujahid attributes it to the unbelievers who denied the messengers, and others take it to refer to God, the jinn or humans, with al-Tabari preferring the first view. The closing phrase, that He encompasses what is with them and has counted everything in number, is read by the exegetes as God's complete knowledge of everything the messengers possess, down to the weight of an atom, according to Ibn Abbas. Commentators also differ on "the one He has approved among the messengers": Ibn Jubayr identifies him as Gabriel, while others take it to mean any prophet to whom God reveals what his mission requires. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi use the verse to deny that saints' miracles involve knowledge of the unseen, whereas al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that it does not exclude them. The verse is also cited against astrology and divination, which Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari reject.

This verse affirms that God alone knows the unseen, and that the only ones to whom He discloses part of it are the messengers He chooses: He reveals to them what He wills of His knowledge, and places guards from the angels before and behind them to shield them from the devils and from eavesdropping. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this guarding serves so that the Prophet may know that the messengers before him had delivered their Lord's message, while Mujahid holds that the knowledge meant is that of those who denied the messengers, and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi report that there were four guardian angels with Gabriel. Commentators differ on who is meant by the subject of the verb 'to know'. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take it to be God Himself, who knows everything in advance but wills that the delivery actually take place, whereas others take it to be the Prophet, the angels, the jinn or Iblis. The phrase 'He has encompassed what is with them and has numbered all things' is read by most as a statement of God's total knowledge, down to the smallest detail. Al-Razi draws from it that what does not exist is not a thing. Some use the passage to condemn divination and astrology and to deny the miracles of saints; al-Alusi and others consider this reading inconclusive, since the verse does not exclude every knowledge of the unseen by others than messengers.
